chapters.title: Chapter 4: Geopolitical Risk and Indian Markets

lessons.title: The Rupee as a Shock Absorber: How RBI Intervention Works During a Crisis

body.text: A weakening rupee is not the RBI failing to do its job. It is often the RBI letting the currency absorb part of a shock deliberately, so the alternative, burning through reserves defending a fixed level, does not become a bigger problem than the shock itself.

children.text: Chapter 1 introduced the rupee's move during a geopolitical shock as part of the currency channel, and the previous chapter's case study showed it absorbing real pressure through 2022. This lesson goes under the hood: what the RBI actually does when the rupee comes under stress, and why its approach is described as managing volatility, not defending a level.
India's Exchange Rate Regime: Managed Float, Not Fixed

body.title: Three Ways a Country Can Run Its Currency

columns.label: Fixed / pegged
points: The central bank commits to a specific exchange rate and defends it directly
Offers stability, but can require enormous reserves to defend during a crisis, and can break suddenly if reserves run out

columns.label: Managed float (India's regime)
points: The market largely sets the rate, but the central bank intervenes to smooth excessive volatility
Allows the currency to absorb part of a shock gradually, rather than requiring the central bank to fight the market head-on
The RBI's stated approach: manage volatility, not defend a specific level

children.text: The RBI's Toolkit During a Crisis

body.caption: How the RBI Manages Rupee Volatility

cells: The RBI directly buys or sells US dollars in the spot market, selling dollars, and absorbing rupees, to slow a sharp depreciation
The RBI uses currency forwards and swaps to influence expectations and liquidity without necessarily moving spot reserves immediately
India's reserve stockpile, the 'war chest' that gives the RBI the firepower to intervene in the first place, built up during calmer periods for exactly this purpose

During acute stress, the RBI has offered concessional swap arrangements to attract NRI dollar deposits into the banking system, a targeted way to bring in fresh foreign currency rather than only spending existing reserves
RBI officials signalling intent or comfort levels publicly, sometimes enough on its own to calm a jittery market without any actual transaction

children.text: Case Study: The 2013 Taper Tantrum and the FCNR(B) Swap Window

body.title: How the RBI Defended the Rupee in 2013

events.title: The Fed signals tapering
events.description: The US Federal Reserve signalled it would start slowing its bond-buying stimulus program, triggering a rapid reversal of capital out of emerging markets globally, an episode now known as the 'Taper Tantrum'.

events.title: The rupee falls sharply
events.description: India, running a large current account deficit and elevated inflation at the time, was labelled one of the 'Fragile Five' emerging economies. The rupee weakened sharply through the year, touching record lows at the time.

events.title: The FCNR(B) swap window opens
events.description: Under incoming RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan, the RBI opened a special concessional swap window for FCNR(B) foreign currency deposits, incentivising banks to raise fresh NRI dollar deposits, which the RBI would swap at an attractive rate.

events.title: Reserves rebuilt, rupee stabilises
events.description: The scheme is widely reported to have mobilised roughly $34 billion in fresh dollar inflows, materially rebuilding reserves and helping the rupee stabilise and partly recover over the following months.

body.text: This case study is worth remembering because it shows the RBI's toolkit going beyond simply selling reserves. Rather than only spending its war chest, it actively brought in fresh dollars through a targeted, temporary incentive, a more creative and arguably more sustainable response than intervention alone.

children.text: Import Cover: The Metric Behind the War Chest

body.label: Import Cover
body.value: Reserves measured in months of imports they could finance
body.context: A commonly watched comfort metric; periods with import cover comfortably above roughly 8 to 9 months are generally seen as reassuring, while a sustained slide toward the 6-month range has historically been flagged as a concern worth monitoring

body.text: Reserves are finite, and intervention alone cannot fix a structural problem. Economists describe this using the 'impossible trinity': a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free movement of capital, and fully independent monetary policy, it can only really have two of the three at once. India's managed float and periodic use of both capital flow and interest rate tools is essentially a practical compromise across this trilemma, not a way of escaping it entirely. If the underlying current account or fiscal picture stays weak, intervention can smooth the path, but it cannot substitute for the structural fix indefinitely.

body.title: Reading an RBI Response
body.scenario: During a geopolitical shock, the rupee weakens sharply. Instead of aggressively selling dollars from reserves, the RBI announces a temporary special deposit scheme to attract fresh NRI dollar inflows, similar in spirit to 2013.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, why might the RBI prefer this approach over simply spending down its existing reserves more heavily?
body.modelAnswer: Spending down existing reserves directly depletes the war chest and signals a defensive, reactive posture, and reserves are finite. A targeted scheme to attract fresh dollar inflows instead brings in new foreign currency, rebuilding rather than depleting reserves, while still relieving pressure on the rupee, similar to how the 2013 FCNR(B) swap window worked. It can be a more sustainable tool during an extended period of stress than spot intervention alone.

body.title: Managed Float vs Fixed
body.question: Under a managed float regime like India's, the RBI's primary stated goal during currency stress is to:
options: Defend a specific fixed exchange rate at all costs
Let the currency move entirely freely with zero intervention
Smooth excessive volatility, without committing to defend a specific level
Fix the exchange rate to the price of gold
body.explanation: A managed float means the market largely determines the exchange rate, while the central bank intervenes selectively to reduce excessive volatility, rather than defending a fixed target level, which is the approach under a pegged regime instead.

cards.definition: An exchange rate regime where the market largely sets the currency's value, but the central bank intervenes periodically to smooth excessive volatility, without defending a fixed target level.

Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits, a scheme allowing NRIs to hold foreign currency deposits in Indian banks, used by the RBI in 2013 through a special swap window to attract fresh dollar inflows during the Taper Tantrum.
A country's foreign exchange reserves measured in the number of months of imports they could finance, a commonly used comfort metric for reserve adequacy.
The economic principle that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and independent monetary policy, it can only sustain two of the three at once.

points: India runs a managed float, where the RBI intervenes to smooth excessive rupee volatility rather than defending a fixed exchange rate level

The RBI's toolkit goes beyond simply selling dollars, spot intervention, forward and swap operations, foreign exchange reserves, targeted NRI deposit schemes, and verbal guidance can all be used depending on the situation

The 2013 Taper Tantrum and the resulting FCNR(B) swap window, which mobilised an estimated $34 billion in fresh dollar inflows, remains the clearest example of the RBI going beyond reserve depletion to actively rebuild its war chest during a crisis
Import cover, reserves measured in months of imports, is a commonly watched comfort metric, with a sustained slide toward roughly 6 months historically flagged as a concern

Intervention has real limits, captured by the 'impossible trinity': a country cannot simultaneously fix its exchange rate, keep capital flows fully open, and run fully independent monetary policy, so intervention can smooth a shock but cannot substitute for fixing a weak structural current account or fiscal position indefinitely

body.text: Figures on the 2013 FCNR(B) inflows and import cover thresholds are approximate, based on widely reported estimates and commonly cited comfort levels that can shift over time. This lesson is educational and not investment advice.
